In both Oranus’s creation of Aphrodite and Ea’s creation of humans, the uniquely male elements of the “birth” illustrate a degree of uniqueness in their progeny that separates them from sexually-born creatures, whether emphasizing irony and the loss of male authority (in Oranous’s case) or creating a species with an imperative in mind and to explain what happened to traitor gods (in the Babylonian case)
After Oranous’s castration at the hands of Chronos, the goddess Aphrodite is formed from his genitals being tossed into the sea. Chronos “swung the fiendishly long and jagged sickle” to prune Oranous’s genitals, which, after floating in the sea, gave rise to Aphrodite. In this case, the man gave birth unintentionally and is a result of Chrono’s and Gaia’s deceit of Oranous. Unlike other male-related births, this one is devoid of a female presence entirely (unlike Zeus’s birth of Athena and Dionysus) and has no element of artistry (dissimilar to Prometheus making humans), and the focus on the male genitalia emphasizes its abnormality. This particular birth is an evolution on the idea that gods don’t die and therefore that no part of them can either that would later become relevant again in the myth of Prometheus and the eagle. The circumstances of the birth also contributes to a sense of irony: the goddess who “loves the organs of sex” and whose dominion includes “the gentle pleasures of sex” was born asexually and through what was anything but a gentle process. As an interesting side note related to the topic of propagation, Oranos essentially disappears from relevance in the Theogony and in the Greek mythological canon as a whole after his castration. He’s not dead, sliced up, or chained in Tartarus but it seems like losing his “manhood” as the Song of Emergence puts it, is probably an accurate term because with its loss, he loses all patriarchy-derived authority that encompasses having multitudes of children; this birth is Oranous’s last and that’s a large part of the reason why he’s replaced. 
	Many of the Babylonian gods are born or created by other gods, including men, and, in fact, it seems like the elements of the created gods emerged more from the minds, rather than the genitalia of their parent, which implies that the parent had some specific idea in mind when creating them, even for the gods that were born “naturally.” For example, in the Enuma Elish, “Anshar made Anu, his offspring, his equal” with the use of “made” implying that Anshar was able to specify that Anu was intended to be equal. Similarly, when Ea “gave birth” to humanity, he was able to specify traits that the humans should have (based on Marduk’s idea), that they “shall bear the gods’ burden that those may rest,'' passing along an imperative and a form to meet that imperative, unlike the greek gods and only like the other gods that were made with an image in mind in the sense that they had a form. This myth, then can be thought of as something of a charter myth, explaining the existence and importance of the human religious institution of serving the gods. Unlike Prometheus, who made humans out of clay, Marduk’s and Ea’s artistic approach to creating humans was to essentially create them by imposing “punishment on [Qingu] and [shedding] his blood” as retribution for his and other gods siding with Tiamat during the war. From the Babylonian perspective, then, humanity made from a male god figure is at least somewhat divine and also part of a divine punishment, taking advantage of the Babylonian gods’ ability to call things into existence to form the rest of humanity around the blood by, for example, “[causing] bones to be,” going into greater anatomical detail than Prometheus did and other human-creator gods often do.

In both versions of the Io story, the irrationality and unfairness of the gods’ culture is highlighted by Zeus violating consent while it is Io that pays the price for his sexual appetites despite not really being an active agent in the myth. In the Ovid story, “Io returning from her father’s stream [h]ad caught Zeus’s eye” and he propositions her in a way that can only be described as commanding (telling her what to do instead of asking her), and when the “girl had run,” he continues to pursue her despite a lack of interest (Ovid, Met., p.18-19). In Prometheus Bound, Zeus is even more malicious, sending “visions…that upset [her] every night” again commandingly propositioning Io even as she continues to stay at home; when she refuses to sleep with him, the oracles that her father sent do Delphi indicated that he “must drive [her] from [her] home and native land…, roaming the remotest regions of the earth” otherwise “Zeus would send a flaming thunderbolt which would destroy his entire race” (Aeschylus, lines 805-821). Zeus uses exile to punish Io for not sleeping with him sooner and the disproportionate threat of violence against the entire race to ensure that she does as he says, which in the case of Prometheus Bound is in line with his characterization by Prometheus as unjust and arbitrary, resorting to extreme measures to maintain a semblance of power when things don’t go his way. 
While both stories do include elements of nonconsent, Aeschylus’ version is tonally much less sympathetic towards the gods, making Zeus and his servants out to be needlessly cruel while Ovid does “redeem” Zeus a little, making him out to be at least somewhat sympathetic. Ovid’s Zeus eventually “could no more endure Io’s distress” and “charged [Mercury] to accomplish Argus’ death,” ideally freeing Io from her confines at the hands of Hera and taking an active role in trying to reduce her suffering, eventually successfully “[pleading] with Juno…to end the punishment” (Ovid, Met., p. 21, 23).  In Prometheus Bound, by contrast, all that is said is “an unexpected fate which no one could foresee robbed [Argus] of his life,” conspicuously omitting any mention of Zeus’ or Hermes’ role in killing Argus (since including that detail would counteract the play’s characterization of Zeus as wholly uncaring); an audience member watching Bound without knowing other versions of the myth would have no indication that Zeus did anything more than exploit Io and forget about her  (Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound, lines 835-836).

The Lovatelli urn appears to depict mysteis undergoing a Elusian mystery ritual. In the scene I re-drew, they are being purified with (presumably) water in a manner similar to Christian baptism to maintain Herakles’ purification when he underwent the ritual in Athens to clean the blood off of himself (as mentioned in class) but also may draw parallels with Hera and other gods washing themselves in Ambrosia. In the Hymn to Demeter, Callimachus lays out what exactly is occurring in the scene and clarifies the point of the rites, declaring that “the mighty, wide-ruling goddess will come to us bringing a white spring…summer, winter, and autumn…as we walk through the city with our feet and heads uncovered so we will forever have feet and heads uninjured…so we will possess gold in abundance” (Trz, p. 76, lines 123-125).This description matches the “first'' scene of the urn (though the urn’s physical cyclicality mirrors the pattern of the seasons and is probably thematically inaccurate to prescribe a beginning point) where initiates and the uninitiated alike walk to the city hall without foot or headwear and implies that the ritual is necessary for Demeter to maintain the cycle of the seasons and provide material wealth for the city. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter also sheds light on the second scene in the urn, showing a parallel between “Demeter anoint[ing] [the child] with ambrosia” and the initiates being purified with water in the ritual (Homer, Trz. p.174). It also speaks to the etiological origin of the ritual depicted, with Demeter commanding the child’s mother to “build [her] a great temple and an alder besides…so that in time you may duly perform [the rites that Demeter assigns] and appease [her] power,” with the events depicted all being from the rites that Demeter prescribes, including sacrificing a pig (Homer, Trz. p. 174).

	In Joseph Campbell’s formulation of the hero’s journey, the descent into the underworld represents the midpoint of the story and narrative serves the purpose of being “the ordeal” which precipitates seizing the sword and fully coming into the overworld a heroic or ascended self. Despite Campbell’s monomyth being derived from greek myths, many protagonists of greek myths do not successfully make it out of the underworld, much less with whatever it is they went in there to get, but, regardless of whether they pass or fail the ordeal, it generally represents the most treacherous point in the journey to acquire the driving force in the narrative, which has interesting parallels with the idea of the underworld as a place of wealth: more than just material wealth, questers like Aeneas or Odysseus can find knowledge and Perithoos can find a spouse, less tangible possessions or qualities. In the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, Orpheus descends into the underworld “because [his] darling wife stepped on a viper that sent through her veins death-poison, cutting off her coming years,” essentially going to the underworld to ask Hades to bring his wife back from the dead (Ovid, Met, book 10). In this text, Eurydice represents both the narrative goal that Orpheus is seeking and a treasure that the underworld has that someone on the surface has to risk through ritual to take. Of course, Orpheus’s doubt and “fear that he might lose her” overwhelms him as, “anxious for another look at her, he turned his eyes so he could gaze upon her” and he returns to the surface empty-handed, a failure that can be looked at through the lens of him being unable to successfully complete the ritual assigned to him by Hades in a profoundly tragic twist of fate where the very love that caused him to come for her caused him to lose her again, an expression of hamartia that is much more characteristic of greek myths than anything in the latter half of Campbell’s model (Ovid, Met, book 10). A point of contrast to Orpheus’ story is Aeneas’ who “journeyed down into the deepest darkness of Erebus to find his father,” though, unlike Orpheus, he doesn’t attempt to bring him back to life as much as he wants to gain knowledge on how to finish his quest, where the knowledge and emotional reconciliation itself is the underworld’s treasure and narrative raison d'être for him (Virgil, Aenead, section 6e from Trz. p. 383). Like, Orpheus’ myth, though, there is great importance placed on rites associated with the journey to the underworld, from “voicing an invocation to Hecate” and sacrificing to her to presenting the golden bough to Charon (Virgil, Aenead, section 6a from Trz. p. 380 and Virgil, Aenead, section 6e from Trz. p. 383).

2/16/22
Athena represents a drastic change in the ancient conception of which powers can be afforded to goddesses in large part because her virginity necessitates that her strength be independent of her ability to produce powerful male heirs or relationship to a god. The most pertinent points of comparison for this are the primordial deities Gaia and Tiamat, both of whom rely on their children to enact their various schemes. In the Theogony, Gaia, seeking revenge on Oranos after he traps their children in the earth, goes to “her dear boys” with a sickle and encourages them “to get even with [their] criminal father” (Hesoid, Theogony, lines 163-165). Rather than get revenge on Oranos directly with her own power, Gaia specifically looks to her male children for help, something Athena is incapable of doing. Similarly, when seeking revenge for Apsu, Tiamat starts biologically producing an army, giving “birth to monster snakes…fierce dragons…hairy hero-men, lion monsters, lion men…scorpion men…” culminating in this Qingu, this male heir to the universe that’s very much in the same vein of Chronos or Typhon - designed to be an instrument of the goddess’s revenge instead of the goddess fighting directly (Enuma Elish, lines 134-140). In contrast, when she fought in the Gigantomachy, she “threw the island of Sicily at Encelados…and she cut the skin off of Pallas,” taking a much more directly active role in the fight than either Gaia or Tiamat did in theirs (Apollodorus, Library, section D1 from Trz. page 22). In Fulgentius’ allegorical interpretation of Athena, he extends this idea that the goddesses have to essentially choose between being physically powerful and having children by pitting Athena’s military skills against Vulcan’s advances, having “to protect her virginity through force of arms” and having to guard her wisdom and qualities that make her an astute fighter against the “fire of passion” (Fulgentius, Myths, section 2.11 from Trz. p. 111).  However, Athena isn’t totally divorced from the primordial goddesses when it comes to settling disputes: like both Gaia and Tiamat who are characterized as scheming or intelligent, she employs cunning and wisdom, being explicitly characterized as “the wise…of the relentless heart” by Homer (Hymn to Athena, from Trz. p 208). She then sits in something of a middle ground regarding gender, fighting in a way that’s more associated with the masculine (though with a strategic bent often associated with goddesses) but also being a patron of weaving and female intelligence. 
	Another aspect of her divergence from the other goddesses is the quality of her strength itself in relation to the gods. While the other goddesses are powerful even without their children, they’re usually characterized as physically weaker than their male counterparts. In the Enuma Elish (line 92), Anshar declares that “a woman’s force may be great but it cannot match a man’s,” and in Metamorphoses (p. 37), Ovid editorializes on Castillo fighting Zeus off, commenting that “she fought as hard as girls can fight…but how could any girl succeed” against their male gods or counterparts. Athena, having “beat Ares and sent him sprawling on the ground”  proves those statements to be false (but, at the same time, further setting herself apart from other female gods) as she not only takes down any male god but her direct, warlike counterpart.

Sappho’s account of the goddess in her Prayer to Aphrodite contrasts with Lucretius’ description of Venus in his work On the Workings of the Universe in that in terms of her importance on cosmic scale and individual relationship with her but, despite varying perceptions on the very construction of Aphrodite, both authors view her as something as a force with which to ally themselves with, though what exactly that entails is far from universal, relying on cultural differences between Greeks and Romans. Lucretius dramatically opens by stating that Venus caused “the ship-bearing sea and the fruitful lands to throng with life” and later that she “alone govern[s] the workings of the universe,” a description that, while clearly derived from her position as the goddess of sex, differs from the Greek understanding (as fertility and the landscape is usually more associated with Demeter or the myths in the Greek canon) through the implication that sex and desire are what ultimately propegate the universe (Lucretius, On the Workings of the Universe, lines 3, 21). Lucretius’ language is very reminiscent of how Cleanthes describes Zeus as an embodiment of logos that is also the “source of all things” who “guides the universal force that pervades all things”; Zeus’ role in Stoicism is then analogous to Venus’ role in Epicureanism and it strengthens her sheer importance on a cosmic scale to followers of the philosophy while also separating her from the anthropomorphization that occurs in myths less associated with a philosophy that makes the god in focus out to be a monolith that reduces how possible it is to have a direct relationship with the goddess (Cleanthes, Hymn to Zeus, lines 2, 12). Sappho’s Aphrodite, rather than be some abstract, all-encompassing notion of sex and desire, is much more in line with the personified, personal gods that can more directly interact with mortals and be bargained with, demonstrated when Aphrotite “[heard Sappho’s] voice from far away…heeded it” and came, having “asked [Sappho] what was wrong” and offered a direct favor to “persuade this time to welcome [her] in friendship” in such a way that suggests a greater interpersonal familiarity or even friendship than what Lucretius has or, because of the greater split between the divine and the mortal in his work, can ever have with his interpretation (Sappho, Prayer to Aphrodite, lines 6-7, 15, 18-19). The reference to Zeus as the king of the universe in the second line of Prayer to Aphrodite and lack of epithets that imply ineffability or more universe-level also indicates that, to Sappho, she isn’t the supreme governing force in the universe like Epicureans believe. Despite that comparative lack of cosmic authority, Sappho still asks Aphrodite to “be [her]self [Sappho’s] ally in arms” to “release [her] from this agony,” paralleling Lucretius’ invocation of similar diction, declaring that he is “eager to have [her] as an ally writing my poetry,” emphasizing Venus’s status as a goddess that mortals ritually call upon through religion or art (like the Muses), though the poets’ reasons for doing so are drastically different: Sappho wants Aphrodite to help her with a personal favor, in line with a more personal relationship with the goddess and Lucretius wants to evangelize his philosophy through his supposedly divinely-inspired poetry, even saying that his poetry is “a work to establish the workings of the universe,” reflecting Venus’ much higher position (Sappho, Hymn to Aphrodite, lines 25-27, Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, lines 24-25).

Justice:
The initial cosmology of the Greco-Roman mythological canon, laid out in the Hesoid’s Theogony and Apollodorus’ Library, uncritically suggests a universe born out of successive acts of brutal, transgenerational retribution. In the early cosmos, justice was essentially a privilege exclusively for figures cunning or strong enough to directly enact it. Consequently, crime and punishment were determined not by legal precedent or moral thought but by the whims of the strongest entity in the situation who themselves were exempt from rule of law; this synonymy between power and authority over justice manifested itself as draconian punishments for crimes that upset the status quo, a criticism of Zeus that Aeschylus levies in Prometheus Bound, or even punishments deflected from the powerful perpetrators of transgressive acts to their victims, such as in the case of the countless women that suffer at the hands of Zeus as described by Ovid in several Metamorphosis passages. Aeschylus offers a final condemnation of the idea of “might is right” in the Oresteia by highlighting the absurdities and contradictions present in retributive justice, and he suggests an alternative, institutional system of justice to break the cycle of revenge. 
Gaia, angry at Ouranos for trapping the hundred-handers and cyclopes underground, becomes the first justice-seeker chronologically, and her immediate response is a violent escalation, claiming to the Titans that the plan to “prune [Ouranos’] genitals” is necessary so that they “might yet get even with [their] criminal father” and further justifying it by pointing out “he started this whole ugly business” (Hesiod, Theogony, lines 181, 165, 167). The diction behind the word “criminal” in describing Ouranos and the discussion of getting even and punishing him points to Gaia using the pretext of justice as an outlet for her ire, stripping him of authority by holding him accountable. Following the gods’ ascension, “Ge, angry about what happened to the Titans” when the gods imprisoned them, attempted justice yet again through generational strength, producing the Giants and Typhon to enact her version of justice and replace cosmic authority but, unlike previous wars between deities, the older generation defeated the younger one (Apollodorus, Library, Section 1.6, lines 1-8). However, the mode of victory,  Zeus’ cunning in “[forbidding] Eos, Selene, and Helios to shine” so that he can “cut the plant” that would make the Giants immortal and his strength that enabled him to “[throw] Mount Aitna…at [Typhon],” remains constant even when that strength and cunning isn’t being used to exact revenge (Apollodorus, Library, Section 1.6.1, lines 10-11, 1.6.3, line 31). The gods are never held accountable for their actions against Ge’s children not because they are necessarily more moral (in fact, their imprisonment of the Titans mirrors the motivation for Gaia to act against the Titans and Ouranos) but because they’re strong enough to simply overpower the supposed agents of justice and cement their authority. This idea of justice through might and militarism may serve as a charter myth for the frequent wars between Greek-city states themselves where domination equates to equity for perceived slights and ceaseless wars between divine powers equates to the constant of mortal war in the ancient Mediterranean with winners being assured of their righteousness (Smith, Jan 19 2022 Myth Theogony, Slide 4).
The ability of autocrats or other powerful entities to arbitrarily define punishments in the name of justice and receive little consequence for their own crimes is a natural consequence of tying the ability to enact justice to the ability to physically or mentally defeat “criminals.” Ovid criticizes the implications of this philosophy in that it would allow autocrats to abuse their power, especially relevant in the context of Augustan Rome, which saw the rise of emperors framing themselves as divine, and his attacks on the emperor through his depiction of Zeus resulted in his exile (Smith, Jan 31 ppt Zeus, Slide 11). In the story of Callisto, Jove “[took] on Diana’s form, her face, and dress” as an opportunity to “seize her,” a blatantly immoral act made even worse through the lens of Roman culture’s preoccupation with women’s sexual purity; however, Jove never receives any punishment for his crimes while Diana “bade [Castillo] quit her company” and Juno enacted “dire revenge,” claiming that “[Castillo’s] joy…[she] shall destroy,” receiving the brunt of the punishment not having committed a crime (Ovid, Metamorphosis, lines 424, 432, 467, 470-477). Because of Jove’s power and authority, he avoids accountability while Juno and Diana punish the victim–an instance of nonsense justice that arises when authority cannot be challenged. 
Similar to Ovid, Aeschylus also criticizes the melding of authority, revenge, and justice, first in Prometheus Bound where Prometheus is eternally tortured for a crime that subverts the status quo of the immortals despite his help in the Titanomachy and Io who, analogously to Castillo, is punished for in lieu of Zeus for being one of his victims (lines 30-48, 250-270, 700-710). Aeschylus’ Oresteia, like the Theogony, centers around a series of revenge-driven acts of violence as Clytemnestra kills Agamemnon for killing their daughter, Orestes kills Clytemnestra to avenge his father, and the Erinyes target Orestes for killing his mother, stressing the lack of resolution that a justice system based on continual murder can ever offer. More compelling, however, are the contradictions that arise when different authorities claiming to represent justice make arbitrary claims about how to enact it: “Apollo’s command…like Fate…directs…[Orestes’] hand towards this collision of killer with killer,” encouraging Orestes to take revenge on Clytemnestra even though “the Furies rise from the blood of a mother,” enacting their distinct form of retributive justice against those that commit matricide (Aeschylus, Oresteia, 2933-2938, 3811). More than just self-perpetuating, power- and authority-driven justice is random and fractured, prompting situations where different gods’ interpretations of justice can pull mortals in disparate directions to their peril. To solve retribution’s problems, Aeschylus, through Athena, advocates for an entirely new judicial system, “[selecting] a jury of the wisest…the first of a permanent court passing judgment on murder…sworn in to integrity and truth”  (Aeschylus, Oresteia, 4739-4744). For the first time, justice is being handed down through institutional means to divorce it from the whims of powerful autocrats, and, furthermore, the jurors are expected to act with wisdom and integrity, a far cry from the base emotion that preempts cycles of murder while also being an etiological explanation and commendation of the Aeropagus’s role as a murder tribunal, upholding the Athenian view of justice (Smith, Eumenides Athena and Orestes, Slide 22). 

Family ties:
	Through a mythological lens, all of science becomes psychology, an analysis of the human-like entities that personify abstract concepts or elements of the natural world and their interactions with each other through their genealogy. However, because the gods are not limited by propriety and often exclusively display the extremes of human fervor, they have both the means and the willingness to express emotions derived from those interactions on a much grander scale than would be humanly possible because of their dual role as anthropomorphized entities and forces of nature, such as Demeter’s actions in the Hymn to Demeter and “Black Demeter” stories where her destructive grief serves an etiological role, shaping nature and ritual, or in “The Story of Vulcan and Minerva” where elements of psychology are created through their conflict. The strife between Jove and Juno in the story of Io shows that such familial relationships have the power to prompt change in addition to creation and destruction. 
	Stories centered around Demeter explore parent-child relationships between gods in a unique, more mortal way. Rather than being static like most gods (including other younger gods like Eros and Ganymede), Persephone both adolesces and metaphorically dies when “against her will, [Hades] seized her and drove her off weeping” to his domain, losing her virginity and marking a transition into married life, predicating a hostile spousal relationship, while also totally isolating her from her past life and becoming as close to death as a god can be, subject to the same fate as the Titans (Homer, Hymn to Demeter, lines 19-20). Demeter, then, is forced to confront the very mortal concern of grief over a child, “[roaming] the earth…in her sorrow” and “wasting away with desire for her…daughter”  as well as the loss of a child to an arranged marriage “by the design of Zeus” (Homer, Hymn to Demeter, lines 48-49, 305-306, 32-33).  Because Demeter is characterized as a mother undergoing loss while also being a god, her grief and anger at Zeus and Hades, emotions informed by her relationships, manifest themselves in the physical world as “the most dread and terrible years…for mortals” because “Demeter…concealed [the seed],” extending the pain she felt to mortals since, because the gods make up the world, any intrafamilial fighting does far more than just strain the relationship between them, resulting in potentially disastrous effects for other beings caught in the crossfire (Homer, Hymn to Demeter, lines 48-49, 305-306, 32-33). The Black Demeter myth elaborates on the idea of gods changing or developing new associations after traumatic events and the dire effects on those unrelated to the squabble. “Demeter, angry with Poseidon” after he forces himself on her during her grief, “put on black raiment and…tarried [in the grotto],” being “surnamed the Black,” essentially given a new epithet that’s more in line with her associations with rage than fertility out of the emotions that arise from being betrayed by all of her brothers (Pausanias, Description of Greece, section 8.42.1, lines 9-10, 3). Because Demeter embodies the harvest, its dying corresponds with a change or possibly metaphorical death in Demeter herself, especially given the parallels between Demeter being unable to find Persephone after her abduction and “none of the other gods…[knowing] where Demeter was hidden” and the fact that the harvest returns once she “abated from her grief” and left the cave (Pausanias, Description of Greece, section 8.42.1, lines 12-13, 19). Because the Hymn to Demeter outlines the etiological reason for the seasons, which occurs as a result of Demeter’s maternal grief and changing between her associations, through Hades’ roles as both a human-like kidnapper and the force of death, the interpersonal conflicts of the divine family and any changes to the gods themselves proceed to alter the workings of the universe.
	Like Demeter’s wrath, the combative spousal relationship between Vulcan and Minerva also extends outside of their marriage. Minerva, married off to Vulcan at Jupiter’s discretion, is “ordered to protect her virginity through force of arms”  and when Vulcan tries to sleep with her, she does that very thing, causing the birth of Erichthonius, “the struggle of envy,” and creating the reason why “every wise man conceals…desire” (Fulgentius, Myths, section 2.11, lines 3-8, 25, 16-17). While not as concrete as the seasons, the idea of the struggle of envy does come from the interplay between Minerva’s embodiment of windom and Vulcan as “the fire of passion…the heat of desire” and those interactions are contextualized through the struggle between spouses, which is much more understandable to the human audience (Fulgentius, Myths, section 2.11, lines 11-12). That battle between the two also affects mortals through the need for the wise to fight off passion-driven madness; even without a physical form, the emotions from familial interactions between the gods can persist and affect mortals. Unlike a simple metaphor or allegory, however, the mythological interpretation treats the story not as a just way of thinking about envy or madness but as the reason why it exists at all. Myth marries the perception of gods as beings with agency and emotion with the gods as the abstract concepts of wisdom and passion whose marital fights and interactions alone can give birth to more entities, whose qualities are derived from their parents, that also exist both in abstraction and in reality. In this way, the gods' genealogy can be extended in ways that don't require sex. 
	In the story of Io, Jove, in the middle of being unfaithful to Juno, “transformed poor Io into a…heifer” to avoid being caught, opening once again on a marital dispute that manifests itself into the physical world: Jove’s infidelity in the relationship is the ineptus that prompts the transformation (Ovid, Metamorphosis, lines 593-617). The idea that Io’s transformation is a real-world embodiment of the problems with Jove’s and Juno’s relationship is confirmed when Jove swore “never again…shall Io give [Juno] cause to grieve” by the Styx, allowing Juno to regain some trust in her husband and, when she does, Io is allowed to return to her normal form (Ovid, Metamorphosis, lines 731-741). Interestingly, Io “is a goddess now,” the use of “now” implying that she wasn’t before, that her experience with Jove, having a child by him and being trapped in the middle of a fight between him and Hera changed her yet again, extending the gods’ genealogy to her through association with Juno’s and Jove’s relationship despite not having a direct blood tie to the Olympians (Ovid, Metamorphosis, line 756

source_rubrics: The response should mention that Aphrodite was born without a maternal presence. For example, it should mention that she was born out of Ouranos's genitalia.
The response should mention the association between women and scheming intelligence. For example, Tiamat's creation of a race of traitor gods.
The response should mention the agency of the primordial goddesses in directing their male children what to do. For example, Gaia's participation in the scheme to get rid of Ouranos.
The response should mention Sappho's interpretation of Aphrodite. For example, it should mention that Sappho characterized Aphrodite as a personified god who could directly interact with mortals.

The response should mention Lucretius' characterization of Venus's relationship with the universe. For example, it should state that Lucretius interpreted Venus as solely governing the universe and that sex and desire are what propagate the universe.
The response should mention the victimization of Persephone. For example, it should state that Persephone was forced into a hostile spousal relationship and became isolated from her past life.
